description.summary: A large winged humanoid creature with glowing red eyes reported in and around Point Pleasant, West Virginia from November 1966 through December 1967. Sightings clustered near the abandoned 'TNT area' of a former World War II munitions plant. The phenomenon culminated, in popular culture, in the December 15, 1967 collapse of the Silver Bridge.
description.full: Mothman is the name given to a winged humanoid figure reported by more than 100 witnesses across the Point Pleasant area of West Virginia during a 13-month period beginning November 15, 1966. The first widely-reported sighting was made by Roger and Linda Scarberry and Steve and Mary Mallette near the abandoned West Virginia Ordnance Works (locally called the 'TNT area'). Witnesses described a roughly 7-foot, grey, humanoid creature with a wingspan of 10 feet and large, intensely glowing red eyes. The name 'Mothman' was coined by an Ohio copy editor as a riff on the popular Batman television series. Reports continued through 1967 and ended after the catastrophic collapse of the Silver Bridge on December 15, 1967, which killed 46 people and bound the creature to a harbinger-of-disaster framing in subsequent folklore. Journalist John Keel's investigations, published as The Mothman Prophecies (1975), tied Mothman to a wider 'Fortean' wave of UFO sightings, Men in Black encounters, and the entity 'Indrid Cold'. Skeptical explanations include misidentification of large North American owls (especially the barred owl) and sandhill cranes, with the eye reflectivity attributed to the tapetum lucidum of nocturnal birds. The town has since embraced Mothman as a cultural icon, with an annual festival and a museum in downtown Point Pleasant.

etymology.origin: The name 'Mothman' was coined by a copy editor at the Mason County Independent (or, in some accounts, an Athens, Ohio newspaper) drawing on the contemporary popularity of the Batman television series, which ran 1966–1968.
etymology.meaning: A portmanteau of 'moth' (for the wings) and 'man' (humanoid posture). Witnesses themselves had described 'a bird' or 'a man with wings'.
etymology.first_use: 1966-11 (Point Pleasant, West Virginia and surrounding press coverage)

features.description: Large red, intensely reflective eyes set in the chest or upper torso area; uniformly the most-cited feature across witnesses
Bat- or moth-like wings with an estimated 10-foot (3 m) span; folded against the back at rest
Walks bipedally and waddles awkwardly; takes off straight up without flapping

features.feature: No visible head or distinct head
features.description: Many witnesses describe the eyes set directly in the upper body without a clearly defined head
Smooth grey skin (some reports) or feathered surface (other reports)

physical.morphology: Reports converge on a roughly human-shaped torso with wings folded behind, but disagree on whether the surface is feathered, leathery, or skin-like.

abilities.description: Reported to take off vertically without wing-flapping and to keep pace with cars driven at 100 mph (160 km/h)
Witnesses describe a paralyzing or mesmerizing sensation upon meeting the creature's eyes
Folkloric reading: appearances precede disaster (most notably the 1967 Silver Bridge collapse)

patterns: Strongly localized to Point Pleasant, West Virginia and the immediate Ohio River Valley
Sightings cluster near the abandoned WW2 munitions area ('TNT area')
Concentrated in a 13-month period (Nov 1966–Dec 1967), then effectively ended

range.description: Sightings centered on Point Pleasant, West Virginia and the immediate Ohio River Valley (Mason County, WV; Gallia County, OH; Meigs County, OH). A small number of contemporaneous reports came from elsewhere in the eastern United States but the canonical wave is local.

hotspots.notes: The bridge collapsed during evening rush on December 15, 1967, killing 46. Mothman sightings effectively ended after the collapse.

first_recorded.source: Earliest report attributed to gravediggers in Clendenin, WV (1966-11-12); the canonical Scarberry/Mallette report follows on 1966-11-15

peak_activity_periods.description: The 'classic' Mothman wave bookended by the Scarberry/Mallette sighting and the Silver Bridge collapse

temporal.seasonal_patterns: Sightings concentrated in late autumn and winter of 1966–67.

origins.cultural_roots: Independent of long folkloric tradition; Mothman is a discrete 1966–67 sighting wave rather than a folkloric figure with deep historical roots. Local folklore retroactively connected the figure to the Curse of Chief Cornstalk (1777), but this connection is post-hoc.
origins.earliest_accounts: November 12, 1966 — gravediggers near Clendenin, West Virginia. November 15, 1966 — the Scarberry/Mallette TNT-area encounter that triggered press coverage.
origins.folklore_connections: Linked by John Keel and later authors to broader harbinger figures (e.g. banshees, Black Aggie) and to the contemporary 1966–67 UFO wave.

history.modern_era: Sightings fully consistent with the 1966–67 description have been rare since the Silver Bridge collapse. The town of Point Pleasant has reframed Mothman as a civic icon, with the Mothman Museum, statue, and annual festival. Skeptical reanalysis (e.g. Joe Nickell) has emphasized the role of large North American owls and the contemporary UFO wave in shaping witness expectations.

notable.name: Scarberry/Mallette TNT-area encounter

location.description: Abandoned West Virginia Ordnance Works ('TNT area'), north of Point Pleasant

notable.description: Roger and Linda Scarberry and Steve and Mary Mallette were driving through the TNT area around midnight when they saw a 6–7 ft tall grey humanoid with large folded wings and bright red glowing eyes near the abandoned generator plant. The creature reportedly took off vertically without flapping its wings and pursued their car at high speed back toward Point Pleasant. They reported the encounter to Deputy Millard Halstead.

conditions.visibility: Headlights and ambient light at the abandoned plant

evidence: Witness statements to Mason County Sheriff

factors: Reported same night to local law enforcement
credibility.notes: The case that triggered the entire wave; effectively the canonical Mothman encounter.

sources: Keel, J. (1975), The Mothman Prophecies, ch. 5

notable.name: Clendenin gravediggers sighting
notable.description: Five men preparing a grave near Clendenin reported a brown human shape with wings flying low overhead from tree to tree. Reported to John Keel during his investigation but received minimal contemporary press.

credibility.notes: Earliest reported sighting of the wave; documentation is retrospective.

notable.name: Connie Carpenter encounter
notable.description: Connie Carpenter was driving on the morning of November 25, 1966 when she encountered the creature on the road. She reported being paralyzed by the gaze of the red eyes for the duration of the encounter, and described eye irritation (later described as sunburn-like) for days afterward.

factors: Reported sunburn-like effect commonly cited in MIB/UFO encounters elsewhere
credibility.notes: Among the most cited individual encounters; central to Keel's account.

notable.name: Silver Bridge collapse and end of wave

location.description: Silver Bridge, Point Pleasant, WV ↔ Kanauga, OH

types: N/A — disaster event, not a sighting

notable.description: The Silver Bridge, a 1928 eyebar suspension bridge, collapsed during evening rush hour, killing 46. NTSB later attributed the collapse to a single eyebar fatigue crack (NTSB HAR-71-1). Mothman sightings effectively ended with the collapse, and folkloric retellings frame the prior 13 months of sightings as harbingers of the disaster.

credibility.notes: Not a Mothman sighting but the historical anchor of the harbinger framing.

paranormal.name: Cornstalk's Curse
paranormal.description: Local folklore frames Mothman as a manifestation of a curse placed on Point Pleasant by the Shawnee chief Cornstalk, murdered by U.S. militia in 1777.
evidence_cited: 1777 murder of Cornstalk at Fort Randolph
Historical disaster cluster in Mason County

skeptical.name: Misidentified barred owl (Strix varia) or other large North American owl
skeptical.description: Witnesses misidentified a startled barred owl (and possibly other Strigidae) flushing from the TNT-area woods. The species' large size, silent flight, glowing red eyeshine, and territorial behavior fit witness descriptions; the TNT area is documented owl habitat.
evidence_cited: Habitat fit (mature deciduous forest of the TNT area)
Witness descriptions of red eyes seen in headlights

skeptical.name: Misidentified sandhill crane
skeptical.description: An out-of-range sandhill crane (Antigone canadensis) was seen in the area in late 1966 according to a contemporary West Virginia naturalist. Its large size (up to 1.2 m tall, 2 m wingspan) and red forehead patch could match witness reports.
evidence_cited: Wingspan and height comparable to witness estimates

skeptical.name: Hoax and mass-hysteria amplification
skeptical.description: The early reports were amplified by press coverage and the contemporary UFO wave, leading to expectation-driven sightings, copycat reports, and a feedback loop sustained by national media (Look magazine, etc.).
evidence_cited: Sharp drop-off in sightings after press attention faded
Sightings concentrated in known media-saturated periods

stories: Indrid Cold and the Woodrow Derenberger encounter (1966-11-02)
folklore.beliefs: Locally, Mothman has shifted from a frightening cryptid to a civic mascot, although the harbinger framing remains in folkloric retellings.

indigenous.significance: The Cornstalk's Curse framing references Shawnee history but is a non-Indigenous folkloric construction. It should not be conflated with Shawnee cosmology.
indigenous.sensitivity_note: The 1777 murder of Cornstalk at Fort Randolph is real history; the curse attribution is a 20th-century folkloric overlay.
indigenous.respect_guidelines: Cite the historical record of Cornstalk's murder accurately; do not present the curse as Shawnee belief.
